Theme B · B2

B2 Programming

How can we apply computer programming to solve problems?

B2.1 Programming fundamentals

This section covers variables, substrings, exception handling, and debugging techniques used in early programming tasks.

B2.1.1 Variables and data types

Variables

A variable is a named location in memory that holds a value. The value can change as the program runs — hence the name. Every variable has three properties you must reason about:

  • Name — an identifier that refers to the stored value. Choose descriptive names (total_score, not x).
  • Type — the kind of data it holds, which determines what operations are valid.
  • Scope — where in the program the variable can be accessed.

Data types

The IB syllabus identifies four fundamental data types:

TypeDescriptionExamples
Integer (int)Whole numbers, positive or negative42, -7, 0
Float (float)Numbers with a decimal point3.14, -0.5, 100.0
Boolean (bool)A logical value: either true or falseTrue, False
String (str)A sequence of characters"hello", "B2", ""

Common mistake

The string "42" and the integer 42 are different types. "42" + "8" produces "428" (concatenation), while 42 + 8 produces 50 (addition). Always be aware of the type you are working with.

Type conversion

Values can be converted between types using casting:

age = int("17")        # string → integer
price = float("9.99")  # string → float
label = str(42)        # integer → string
flag = bool(1)         # integer → boolean (True)

Type conversion is essential when reading user input, since input() always returns a string.

Variable scope

Scope determines where a variable can be used.

A local variable is declared inside a function and exists only within that function. Once the function finishes, the variable is destroyed.

A global variable is declared outside all functions and can be read from anywhere in the program. To modify a global variable inside a function, you must explicitly declare it with the global keyword.

score = 0                # global variable

def add_points(points):
    global score
    score = score + points  # modifies the global variable

def show_local():
    result = 10            # local variable
    print(result)

show_local()              # prints 10
# print(result)           # ERROR: result does not exist here

Best practice

Overusing global variables makes programs harder to understand and debug, because any part of the program can change them. Prefer passing values as function parameters and returning results. Use globals only when genuinely necessary.

Worked example

Tracing variables through a program

x = 5
y = x + 3
x = y * 2
y = x - y
Linexy
x = 55—
y = x + 358
x = y * 2168
y = x - y168

Final values: x = 16, y = 8.

Key takeaways — B2.1.1

  • Variables store values that can change during execution. Each has a name, type, and scope.
  • Four fundamental data types: integer, float, boolean, string.
  • Type conversion (casting) is needed when operations require a specific type.
  • Local variables exist only inside the function that declares them; global variables are accessible everywhere but should be used sparingly.

B2.1.2 String manipulation

Strings are sequences of characters. Each character has an index, starting from 0. String manipulation is a core programming skill tested frequently in the IB.

Accessing characters and substrings

name = "Computer"
print(name[0])      # "C"  — first character
print(name[3])      # "p"  — fourth character
print(name[-1])     # "r"  — last character

A substring is a portion of a string, extracted using slicing:

text = "Computer Science"
print(text[0:8])     # "Computer"  — index 0 up to (not including) 8
print(text[9:])      # "Science"   — index 9 to the end
print(text[:4])      # "Comp"      — start to index 4

Common string operations

OperationPython syntaxExampleResult
Lengthlen(s)len("hello")5
Concatenations1 + s2"hello" + " world""hello world"
Uppercases.upper()"hello".upper()"HELLO"
Lowercases.lower()"HELLO".lower()"hello"
Find substrings.find(sub)"hello".find("ll")2
Replaces.replace(old, new)"hello".replace("l", "r")"herro"
Splits.split(sep)"a,b,c".split(",")["a", "b", "c"]
Strip whitespaces.strip()" hi ".strip()"hi"

Worked example

Extracting initials from a full name

full_name = "Ada Lovelace"
parts = full_name.split(" ")
initials = parts[0][0] + parts[1][0]
print(initials)  # "AL"

split(" ") breaks the string at each space, producing ["Ada", "Lovelace"]. Accessing [0] of each part gives the first character.

Common mistake

String indices start at 0, not 1. In the string "Code", the character at index 1 is "o", not "C". Off-by-one errors are the most frequent string-handling bug.

Key takeaways — B2.1.2

  • Strings are indexed from 0. Use square brackets to access individual characters.
  • Slicing extracts substrings: s[start:end] includes start but excludes end.
  • Key methods: len(), upper(), lower(), find(), replace(), split(), strip().
  • Concatenation joins strings with +.

B2.1.3 Exception handling

An exception is an error that occurs while a program is running. Unlike syntax errors (which prevent the program from starting), exceptions happen during execution — for example, dividing by zero, converting an invalid string to a number, or accessing an index that does not exist.

Without handling, an exception causes the program to crash with an error message. Exception handling allows the program to catch the error and respond gracefully.

The try/except pattern

try:
    age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
    print("You are", age, "years old")
except ValueError:
    print("That is not a valid number")

If the user enters "seventeen", int() raises a ValueError. The except block catches it and prints a helpful message instead of crashing.

Common exception types

ExceptionCauseExample
ValueErrorInvalid value for the expected typeint("hello")
TypeErrorWrong type used in an operation"5" + 3
ZeroDivisionErrorDivision or modulo by zero10 / 0
IndexErrorIndex out of range[1, 2, 3][5]
FileNotFoundErrorFile does not existopen("missing.txt")

Multiple except blocks

try:
    numbers = [10, 20, 30]
    index = int(input("Enter index: "))
    print(numbers[index])
except ValueError:
    print("Please enter a whole number")
except IndexError:
    print("Index out of range — valid indices are 0, 1, 2")

The else and finally clauses

try:
    value = int(input("Enter a number: "))
except ValueError:
    print("Invalid input")
else:
    print("You entered:", value)   # runs only if no exception occurred
finally:
    print("Input attempt complete")  # always runs, regardless

Why exception handling matters

Exception handling is not just about preventing crashes. It makes programs more robust and user-friendly. A well-handled exception provides a clear error message and allows the user to try again, rather than losing all their work to a crash.

Key takeaways — B2.1.3

  • Exceptions are runtime errors that disrupt normal execution.
  • try/except blocks catch exceptions and provide controlled responses.
  • Common exceptions: ValueError, TypeError, ZeroDivisionError, IndexError.
  • Use else for code that should run only when no error occurs; use finally for cleanup that must always run.

B2.1.4 Debugging techniques

Debugging is the process of finding and fixing errors in code. Effective debugging requires understanding the three categories of error and applying systematic techniques.

Error categories

Syntax error

A violation of the programming language's grammar rules. The code cannot run at all. Examples: missing colons, unmatched brackets, misspelled keywords. The interpreter or compiler reports the location and nature of the error.

Runtime error

An error that occurs during execution, causing the program to crash. The code is syntactically correct but encounters an impossible operation. Examples: dividing by zero, accessing an invalid index, opening a missing file.

Logic error

The program runs without crashing but produces incorrect results due to flawed reasoning. Examples: using the wrong operator (+ instead of -), an off-by-one loop boundary, an incorrect condition. Logic errors are the hardest to find because the program gives no error message.

Debugging techniques

Print statements — inserting print() calls at key points to display variable values and execution flow. Simple but effective for tracking down where values diverge from expectations.

def calculate_average(numbers):
    total = 0
    for num in numbers:
        total += num
        print(f"num={num}, total={total}")  # debugging output
    average = total / len(numbers)
    print(f"average={average}")             # check final result
    return average

Trace tables — a structured record of variable values at each step. Particularly useful for loop-based algorithms. Create a column for each variable and a row for each step, recording every change.

Breakpoints and stepping — most IDEs allow you to set breakpoints that pause execution at a specific line. You can then step through the code line by line, inspecting variable values at each point. This is more efficient than print statements for complex programs.

Rubber duck debugging — explaining the code line by line to someone (or something) else. The act of articulating what each line should do often reveals where the logic breaks down.

A systematic approach

  1. Reproduce the error with specific input that triggers it.
  2. Isolate the location — use error messages, print statements, or breakpoints to narrow down where the problem occurs.
  3. Understand why the error happens — read the code carefully and trace through the logic.
  4. Fix the error and verify that the fix works with the original input.
  5. Test with additional inputs to ensure the fix does not introduce new problems.

Common mistake

Changing code randomly until the problem disappears is not debugging. It often introduces new bugs and does not build understanding. Always diagnose the root cause before changing code.

Key takeaways — B2.1.4

  • Syntax errors prevent the program from running; runtime errors crash during execution; logic errors produce wrong results silently.
  • Key techniques: print statements, trace tables, breakpoints and stepping, rubber duck debugging.
  • Debugging should be systematic: reproduce, isolate, understand, fix, test.

B2.2 Data structures

This section covers static and dynamic structures, arrays, lists, stacks, and queues used in practical programming problems.

B2.2.1 Static and dynamic data structures

A data structure is a way of organising data so it can be accessed and modified efficiently. The choice of data structure affects both the performance and the clarity of a program. The IB distinguishes between two categories.

Static data structure

A structure whose size is fixed when it is created and cannot change during execution. Memory is allocated as a single contiguous block. Example: a fixed-size array.

Dynamic data structure

A structure that can grow or shrink during execution as data is added or removed. Memory is allocated on demand and may not be contiguous. Examples: linked lists, Python lists.

Comparison

FeatureStaticDynamic
SizeFixed at creationGrows and shrinks as needed
Memory allocationOne contiguous blockAllocated on demand
Memory efficiencyMay waste space if not fullUses only what is needed (plus pointer overhead)
Access speedFast — direct index accessMay be slower (depends on structure)
Insertion/deletionSlow — elements may need shiftingCan be fast (e.g. linked list insertion)
PredictabilityMemory use is predictableMemory use varies at runtime

Python note

Python's built-in list is technically a dynamic array — it resizes automatically. In the IB context, treat Python lists as dynamic structures and fixed-size arrays (as found in Java or C) as static structures.

Key takeaways — B2.2.1

  • Static structures have a fixed size set at creation; dynamic structures resize during execution.
  • Static structures offer fast direct access but may waste memory; dynamic structures are flexible but carry overhead.
  • Choose based on whether the data size is known in advance and whether fast insertion/deletion is needed.

B2.2.2 Arrays and lists

Arrays

An array is an ordered collection of elements of the same type, stored in contiguous memory. Each element is accessed by its index, starting from 0. Arrays have a fixed size — once created, you cannot add or remove elements.

In many languages (Java, C++), arrays are declared with a fixed length:

// Pseudocode
DECLARE scores : ARRAY[5] OF INTEGER
scores[0] ← 85
scores[1] ← 92

Lists (Python)

In Python, the list type serves as a dynamic array. Lists can hold mixed types, grow and shrink, and support a wide range of operations:

scores = [85, 92, 78, 95, 88]
scores.append(91)        # add to end → [85, 92, 78, 95, 88, 91]
scores.insert(2, 100)    # insert at index 2
scores.remove(78)        # remove first occurrence of 78
scores.pop()             # remove and return last element

Common list operations

OperationPython syntaxDescription
Access elementlst[i]Get element at index i
Update elementlst[i] = valSet element at index i
Appendlst.append(val)Add element to end
Insertlst.insert(i, val)Insert at index i
Removelst.remove(val)Remove first occurrence
Poplst.pop()Remove and return last element
Lengthlen(lst)Number of elements
Sortlst.sort()Sort in ascending order
Searchval in lstReturns True if found

Two-dimensional arrays

A 2D array stores data in rows and columns, like a table or grid:

grid = [
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6],
    [7, 8, 9]
]
print(grid[1][2])  # 6 — row 1, column 2

To traverse a 2D array, use nested loops:

for row in range(len(grid)):
    for col in range(len(grid[row])):
        print(grid[row][col], end=" ")
    print()

Key takeaways — B2.2.2

  • Arrays are fixed-size, same-type collections accessed by index (starting at 0).
  • Python lists are dynamic and support append, insert, remove, pop, sort, and search.
  • 2D arrays store grid-like data and are accessed with two indices: [row][col].

B2.2.3 The stack

A stack is a data structure that follows the last-in, first-out (LIFO) principle. The most recently added item is the first to be removed — like a stack of plates where you always take from the top.

Stack operations

OperationDescription
PushAdd an item to the top of the stack
PopRemove and return the item from the top
PeekView the top item without removing it
isEmptyCheck whether the stack is empty
isFullCheck whether the stack is full (for bounded stacks)

Common mistake

Overflow occurs when you try to push onto a full stack. Underflow occurs when you try to pop from an empty stack. Always check before performing these operations.

Implementing a stack in Python

stack = []

# Push
stack.append("A")
stack.append("B")
stack.append("C")
print(stack)  # ["A", "B", "C"]

# Peek
print(stack[-1])  # "C" — top of stack

# Pop
top = stack.pop()
print(top)    # "C"
print(stack)  # ["A", "B"]

Real-world uses of stacks

  • Undo functionality — each action is pushed onto a stack; pressing undo pops the most recent action.
  • Browser back button — visited pages are pushed onto a stack; pressing back pops the most recent page.
  • Function call stack — when a function calls another function, the current state is pushed onto the call stack and restored when the called function returns.
  • Expression evaluation — compilers use stacks to evaluate mathematical expressions and check bracket matching.

Worked example

Tracing stack operations

OperationStack (top → right)Returned
push(10)[10]—
push(20)[10, 20]—
push(30)[10, 20, 30]—
pop()[10, 20]30
peek()[10, 20]20
pop()[10]20
pop()[]10
pop()[] — UNDERFLOWError

Key takeaways — B2.2.3

  • A stack follows LIFO: the last item added is the first removed.
  • Core operations: push (add), pop (remove), peek (view top), isEmpty, isFull.
  • Overflow = pushing onto a full stack; underflow = popping from an empty stack.
  • Stacks are used for undo systems, browser history, function calls, and expression evaluation.

B2.2.4 The queue

A queue is a data structure that follows the first-in, first-out (FIFO) principle. The first item added is the first to be removed — like a queue of people waiting in line.

Queue operations

OperationDescription
EnqueueAdd an item to the rear of the queue
DequeueRemove and return the item from the front
Peek / FrontView the front item without removing it
isEmptyCheck whether the queue is empty
isFullCheck whether the queue is full (for bounded queues)

Implementing a queue in Python

from collections import deque

queue = deque()

# Enqueue
queue.append("A")
queue.append("B")
queue.append("C")
print(queue)  # deque(["A", "B", "C"])

# Peek
print(queue[0])  # "A" — front of queue

# Dequeue
front = queue.popleft()
print(front)   # "A"
print(queue)   # deque(["B", "C"])

Why deque?

Python's regular list can be used as a queue with append() and pop(0), but pop(0) is slow because it shifts all remaining elements. collections.deque provides efficient operations at both ends.

Real-world uses of queues

  • Print queues — documents are printed in the order they are submitted.
  • CPU scheduling — processes wait in a ready queue for their turn to execute (round-robin scheduling uses a queue).
  • Message queues — systems process incoming messages in order.
  • Breadth-first search — graph traversal algorithms use a queue to explore nodes level by level.

Worked example

Tracing queue operations

OperationQueue (front → left)Returned
enqueue("X")[X]—
enqueue("Y")[X, Y]—
enqueue("Z")[X, Y, Z]—
dequeue()[Y, Z]X
enqueue("W")[Y, Z, W]—
dequeue()[Z, W]Y
peek()[Z, W]Z

Stack vs queue comparison

FeatureStack (LIFO)Queue (FIFO)
AddPush (top)Enqueue (rear)
RemovePop (top)Dequeue (front)
OrderLast in, first outFirst in, first out
AnalogyStack of platesQueue of people
Use caseUndo, backtrackingScheduling, buffering

Key takeaways — B2.2.4

  • A queue follows FIFO: the first item added is the first removed.
  • Core operations: enqueue (add to rear), dequeue (remove from front), peek, isEmpty.
  • Queues are used for print spooling, CPU scheduling, message processing, and breadth-first search.
  • Stacks and queues differ in ordering: LIFO vs FIFO.

B2.3 Programming constructs

This section focuses on sequencing, selection, looping, and modular functions as the backbone of structured programs.

B2.3.1 Sequence

Sequence is the simplest programming construct: instructions are executed one after another, in the order they are written. Every program relies on sequence as its foundation.

name = input("Enter your name: ")
greeting = "Hello, " + name
print(greeting)

The three lines execute in strict order. If the order were changed — for example, printing before reading the input — the program would fail or produce incorrect output.

Why sequence matters

Sequence errors are common and subtle. If you calculate a value after you use it, the program may run without crashing but produce incorrect results — a logic error that can be hard to detect.

Key takeaways — B2.3.1

  • Sequence means executing instructions in the order they are written.
  • The order of statements affects correctness — variables must be assigned before they are used.

B2.3.2 Selection

Selection allows a program to choose between different paths based on a condition. The condition is evaluated, and the path taken depends on whether it is true or false.

if / elif / else

score = int(input("Enter score: "))

if score >= 90:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 80:
    grade = "B"
elif score >= 70:
    grade = "C"
else:
    grade = "F"

print("Grade:", grade)
  • if tests the first condition.
  • elif (else if) tests additional conditions, checked in order.
  • else catches everything not matched by the conditions above.
  • Only one branch executes — once a condition is true, the remaining branches are skipped.

Comparison and logical operators

OperatorMeaningExample
==Equal tox == 5
!=Not equal tox != 0
<Less thanx < 10
>Greater thanx > 0
<=Less than or equalx <= 100
>=Greater than or equalx >= 18
andBoth conditions truex > 0 and x < 100
orAt least one condition truex < 0 or x > 100
notInverts the conditionnot found

Nested selection

Selection structures can be placed inside each other for more complex decision-making:

age = int(input("Enter age: "))
has_licence = input("Do you have a licence? (y/n): ")

if age >= 17:
    if has_licence == "y":
        print("You can drive")
    else:
        print("You need to get a licence first")
else:
    print("You are too young to drive")

Common mistake

Using = (assignment) instead of == (comparison) in a condition is one of the most frequent selection errors. In Python, if x = 5 is a syntax error, but in some other languages it silently assigns the value, causing a hard-to-find logic bug.

Key takeaways — B2.3.2

  • Selection uses if, elif, and else to choose between execution paths based on conditions.
  • Conditions use comparison operators (==, !=, <, >) and logical operators (and, or, not).
  • Only one branch of an if/elif/else chain executes.
  • Selection structures can be nested for complex decisions.

B2.3.3 Iteration

Iteration means repeating a block of code. There are two main forms.

Count-controlled loops (for)

A count-controlled loop runs a known number of times:

for i in range(5):
    print(i)     # prints 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

for i in range(2, 10, 3):
    print(i)     # prints 2, 5, 8

range(start, stop, step) generates numbers from start up to (but not including) stop, incrementing by step.

Condition-controlled loops (while)

A condition-controlled loop repeats while a condition is true:

password = ""
while password != "secret":
    password = input("Enter password: ")
print("Access granted")

The loop continues until the user enters the correct password. If the condition is false from the start, the loop body never executes.

Common mistake

An infinite loop occurs when the loop condition never becomes false. This usually happens because the variable in the condition is never updated inside the loop body. Always ensure something inside the loop moves toward termination.

Nested loops

A loop inside another loop is a nested loop. The inner loop completes all its iterations for each single iteration of the outer loop:

for row in range(3):
    for col in range(4):
        print("*", end=" ")
    print()

This prints a 3 × 4 grid of asterisks. The inner loop runs 4 times for each of the 3 outer iterations — 12 print operations in total.

Iterating through collections

names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"]
for name in names:
    print(name)

for i in range(len(names)):
    print(f"Index {i}: {names[i]}")

Key takeaways — B2.3.3

  • for loops are count-controlled — use when the number of iterations is known.
  • while loops are condition-controlled — use when the number of iterations depends on a condition.
  • Nested loops multiply: an outer loop of m iterations with an inner loop of n iterations runs the inner body m × n times.
  • Always ensure loop conditions can become false to avoid infinite loops.

B2.3.4 Functions and modularisation

A function is a named, reusable block of code that performs a specific task. Functions are the primary tool for modularisation — breaking a program into smaller, manageable, testable pieces.

Defining and calling functions

def calculate_area(length, width):
    area = length * width
    return area

result = calculate_area(5, 3)
print(result)  # 15
  • def declares the function with a name and parameters (inputs).
  • The function body contains the instructions to execute.
  • return sends a value back to the calling code.
  • Arguments are the actual values passed when the function is called.

Functions without return values

Not every function needs to return a value. Functions that perform an action (like printing) without returning data are sometimes called procedures:

def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

greet("Alice")  # prints "Hello, Alice!"

Why modularisation matters

  • Readability — a well-named function describes what a section of code does without you reading every line.
  • Reusability — write the logic once and call it from multiple places.
  • Testability — each function can be tested independently.
  • Collaboration — different team members can work on different functions.
  • Maintenance — fixing a bug in a function fixes it everywhere the function is used.

Worked example

Modularising a grade calculator

def get_grade(score):
    if score >= 90:
        return "A"
    elif score >= 80:
        return "B"
    elif score >= 70:
        return "C"
    else:
        return "F"

def process_student(name, score):
grade = get_grade(score)
print(f”{name}: {grade}”)


process_student(“Alice”, 85)   # Alice: B
process_student(“Bob”, 92)     # Bob: A
process_student(“Charlie”, 68) # Charlie: F

Each function has one clear responsibility. get_grade() handles the grading logic; process_student() handles the output. If the grading boundaries change, only get_grade() needs updating.

Key takeaways — B2.3.4

  • Functions are named, reusable code blocks with parameters, a body, and an optional return value.
  • Modularisation improves readability, reusability, testability, and maintenance.
  • Each function should have one clear responsibility.
  • Parameters are the names in the definition; arguments are the values passed when calling.

B2.4 Programming algorithms

This section covers Big O, linear and binary search, sort algorithms, and the HL recursion extension.

B2.4.1 Algorithm efficiency and Big O notation

Not all algorithms that solve the same problem are equally efficient. Big O notation provides a way to describe how an algorithm’s performance scales as the input size increases.

Big O focuses on the growth rate, not the exact number of operations. It answers the question: “If I double the input size, how much longer does the algorithm take?”

Common Big O complexities

NotationNameGrowthExample
O(1)ConstantSame time regardless of input sizeAccessing an array element by index
O(log n)LogarithmicDoubles input → one extra stepBinary search
O(n)LinearDoubles input → double the timeLinear search
O(n log n)LinearithmicEfficient sortingMerge sort
O(n²)QuadraticDoubles input → four times the timeBubble sort, selection sort
O(2ⁿ)ExponentialGrows extremely fastBrute-force password cracking

How to determine Big O

Count the dominant operation (usually comparisons or assignments) as a function of input size n. A single loop through n items is O(n). A nested loop where both iterate over n items is O(n²). Constant operations outside loops are O(1) and are ignored when a larger term exists.

Worked example

Comparing O(n) and O(n²) growth

n (input size)O(n) operationsO(n²) operations
1010100
10010010,000
1,0001,0001,000,000
10,00010,000100,000,000

At small input sizes the difference is negligible. At 10,000 items, the O(n²) algorithm performs 10,000 times more operations than the O(n) algorithm. This is why efficiency matters.

Key takeaways — B2.4.1

  • Big O describes how an algorithm's performance scales with input size.
  • Common complexities, from fastest to slowest: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ).
  • A single loop is typically O(n); a nested loop is O(n²); halving the search space each step is O(log n).

B2.4.2 Searching algorithms

Linear search

Linear search checks each element in order, starting from the first, until the target is found or the end is reached.

def linear_search(data, target):
    for i in range(len(data)):
        if data[i] == target:
            return i       # found — return the index
    return -1              # not found

Time complexity: O(n) — in the worst case, every element is checked.

Advantages: works on unsorted data; simple to implement.

Disadvantages: slow for large datasets.

Worked example

Tracing linear search

Search for 7 in [3, 8, 1, 7, 5].

idata[i]data[i] == 7?
03No
18No
21No
37Yes → return 3

Found at index 3 after 4 comparisons.

Binary search

Binary search works only on sorted data. It repeatedly compares the target to the middle element and eliminates half the remaining data each time.

def binary_search(data, target):
    low = 0
    high = len(data) - 1
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if data[mid] == target:
            return mid
        elif data[mid] < target:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid - 1
    return -1

Time complexity: O(log n) — each comparison halves the search space.

Advantages: very fast for large sorted datasets.

Disadvantages: requires sorted data; more complex to implement.

Worked example

Tracing binary search

Search for 23 in [5, 10, 15, 20, 23, 30, 35].

Steplowhighmiddata[mid]Action
10632023 > 20 → low = 4
24653023 < 30 → high = 4
344423Found → return 4

Found at index 4 after only 3 comparisons (linear search would need 5).

Comparing linear and binary search

FeatureLinear searchBinary search
Requires sorted data?NoYes
Time complexityO(n)O(log n)
Best caseO(1) — first elementO(1) — middle element
Suitable forSmall or unsorted datasetsLarge sorted datasets
ImplementationSimpleMore complex

Key takeaways — B2.4.2

  • Linear search checks every element in order — O(n), works on unsorted data.
  • Binary search halves the search space each step — O(log n), requires sorted data.
  • For large datasets, binary search is dramatically faster, but the data must be sorted first.

B2.4.3 Sorting algorithms

Bubble sort

Bubble sort repeatedly passes through the list, comparing adjacent elements and swapping them if they are in the wrong order. After each pass, the largest unsorted element “bubbles up” to its correct position.

def bubble_sort(data):
    n = len(data)
    for i in range(n - 1):
        for j in range(n - 1 - i):
            if data[j] > data[j + 1]:
                data[j], data[j + 1] = data[j + 1], data[j]
    return data

Time complexity: O(n²) — even in the average case.

Worked example

Tracing bubble sort

Sort [5, 3, 8, 1].

Pass 1:

  • Compare 5, 3 → swap → [3, 5, 8, 1]
  • Compare 5, 8 → no swap → [3, 5, 8, 1]
  • Compare 8, 1 → swap → [3, 5, 1, 8]

Pass 2:

  • Compare 3, 5 → no swap → [3, 5, 1, 8]
  • Compare 5, 1 → swap → [3, 1, 5, 8]

Pass 3:

  • Compare 3, 1 → swap → [1, 3, 5, 8]

Result: [1, 3, 5, 8]. Three passes needed for four elements.

Selection sort

Selection sort divides the list into a sorted portion (initially empty) and an unsorted portion. On each pass, it finds the smallest element in the unsorted portion and swaps it into the next position.

def selection_sort(data):
    n = len(data)
    for i in range(n - 1):
        min_index = i
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if data[j] < data[min_index]:
                min_index = j
        data[i], data[min_index] = data[min_index], data[i]
    return data

Time complexity: O(n²) — always makes the same number of comparisons.

Worked example

Tracing selection sort

Sort [5, 3, 8, 1].

Pass 1: Find minimum in [5, 3, 8, 1] → 1 at index 3. Swap with index 0 → [1, 3, 8, 5]

Pass 2: Find minimum in [3, 8, 5] → 3 at index 1. Already in place → [1, 3, 8, 5]

Pass 3: Find minimum in [8, 5] → 5 at index 3. Swap with index 2 → [1, 3, 5, 8]

Result: [1, 3, 5, 8].

Comparing bubble sort and selection sort

FeatureBubble sortSelection sort
Time complexityO(n²)O(n²)
Number of swapsMany (every adjacent pair)Few (one per pass)
Best caseO(n) with early terminationO(n²) — always scans fully
StabilityStable (preserves order of equal elements)Not stable by default
MemoryIn-place (O(1) extra space)In-place (O(1) extra space)

Neither is efficient for large data

Both bubble sort and selection sort are O(n²), which makes them impractical for large datasets. More efficient algorithms like merge sort (O(n log n)) exist but are not required at SL. The IB tests these algorithms because they are simple enough to trace by hand and illustrate key algorithmic concepts.

Key takeaways — B2.4.3

  • Bubble sort compares and swaps adjacent elements repeatedly — O(n²), many swaps.
  • Selection sort finds the minimum unsorted element and places it next — O(n²), fewer swaps.
  • Both are O(n²) and suitable only for small datasets, but they are important to understand and trace.
  • You must be able to trace both algorithms step by step for given data.

HL extension

B2.4.4 The concept of recursion

Recursion is a problem-solving technique where a function solves a problem by calling itself with a smaller or simpler version of the same problem. The process continues until it reaches a base case — a condition where the answer is known directly and no further recursion is needed.

Structure of a recursive function

Every recursive function has two essential parts:

  1. Base case — the condition that stops the recursion and returns a known value directly.
  2. Recursive case — the function calls itself with a modified (usually smaller) input, moving toward the base case.

If the base case is missing or never reached, the function calls itself indefinitely until the system runs out of memory — a stack overflow.

How recursion works: the call stack

Each time a function calls itself, the current state (local variables, parameters, return address) is pushed onto the call stack. When a base case is reached, the function returns a value, and the stack unwinds — each waiting call receives its result and returns in turn.

Worked example

Factorial using recursion

The factorial of n (written n!) is defined as:

  • Base case: 0! = 1
  • Recursive case: n! = n × (n − 1)!
def factorial(n):
    if n == 0:          # base case
        return 1
    else:               # recursive case
        return n * factorial(n - 1)

Tracing factorial(4):

CallnActionReturns
factorial(4)44 × factorial(3)waits...
factorial(3)33 × factorial(2)waits...
factorial(2)22 × factorial(1)waits...
factorial(1)11 × factorial(0)waits...
factorial(0)0base case1

Unwinding: factorial(1) returns 1×1=1, factorial(2) returns 2×1=2, factorial(3) returns 3×2=6, factorial(4) returns 4×6=24.

Recursion vs iteration

Any recursive algorithm can be rewritten as an iterative one (using loops), and vice versa. The choice depends on clarity and suitability.

FeatureRecursionIteration
Code clarityOften cleaner for naturally recursive problems (trees, fractals)Better for simple counting or traversal
Memory useUses the call stack — risk of stack overflow for deep recursionUses constant extra memory
PerformanceFunction call overhead on each recursionGenerally faster
When to useTree traversal, divide-and-conquer, mathematical definitionsLinear processing, simple loops

Common mistake

Forgetting the base case or not making the recursive call move toward it causes infinite recursion. In Python, this produces a RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded. Always verify that the recursive case reduces the problem toward the base case.

Key takeaways — B2.4.4

  • Recursion solves a problem by having a function call itself with a smaller input.
  • Every recursive function needs a base case (stops recursion) and a recursive case (calls itself).
  • Each recursive call is stored on the call stack; the stack unwinds when the base case is reached.
  • Recursion trades memory (call stack) for code clarity — use it when the problem is naturally recursive.

B2.4.5 Constructing recursive algorithms

At HL, you must be able to construct and trace recursive solutions — not just understand the concept. This section demonstrates recursive approaches to common problems.

Fibonacci sequence

The Fibonacci sequence is defined as: F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1, F(n) = F(n−1) + F(n−2).

def fibonacci(n):
    if n <= 0:
        return 0           # base case
    elif n == 1:
        return 1           # base case
    else:
        return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2)  # recursive case

Efficiency warning

This naive recursive Fibonacci is O(2ⁿ) because it recalculates the same sub-problems many times. For fibonacci(5), fibonacci(2) is calculated three separate times. Techniques like memoisation (caching results) eliminate this redundancy, but that is beyond IB scope.

Sum of a list

def recursive_sum(lst):
    if len(lst) == 0:       # base case: empty list
        return 0
    else:                    # recursive case: first element + sum of rest
        return lst[0] + recursive_sum(lst[1:])

Worked example

Tracing recursive_sum([3, 7, 2])

CalllstActionReturns
recursive_sum([3, 7, 2])[3, 7, 2]3 + recursive_sum([7, 2])waits...
recursive_sum([7, 2])[7, 2]7 + recursive_sum([2])waits...
recursive_sum([2])[2]2 + recursive_sum([])waits...
recursive_sum([])[]base case0

Unwinding: 2+0=2, 7+2=9, 3+9=12.

Recursive binary search

def binary_search_recursive(data, target, low, high):
    if low > high:
        return -1                          # base case: not found
    mid = (low + high) // 2
    if data[mid] == target:
        return mid                         # base case: found
    elif data[mid] < target:
        return binary_search_recursive(data, target, mid + 1, high)
    else:
        return binary_search_recursive(data, target, low, mid - 1)

This mirrors the iterative binary search but replaces the while loop with recursive calls, each narrowing the search range.

Power function

def power(base, exp):
    if exp == 0:             # base case: anything to the power 0 is 1
        return 1
    else:                    # recursive case
        return base * power(base, exp - 1)

power(2, 4) → 2 × power(2, 3) → 2 × 2 × power(2, 2) → 2 × 2 × 2 × power(2, 1) → 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × power(2, 0) → 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 1 = 16.

Key takeaways — B2.4.5

  • You must be able to write and trace recursive solutions for problems like factorial, Fibonacci, list summation, and binary search.
  • Identify the base case (when to stop) and the recursive case (how to reduce the problem) before coding.
  • Trace by listing each call, showing what it waits for, and then unwinding the return values.

B2.5 File processing

This section focuses on opening, reading, writing, appending, and closing files accurately in code.

B2.5.1 File-processing operations

Programs store data in variables, but variables exist only while the program is running. To keep data between sessions, programs must read from and write to persistent storage — files on disk.

Opening and closing files

Before reading or writing, a file must be opened with a specified mode:

ModeDescription
"r"Read — open an existing file for reading. Error if the file does not exist.
"w"Write — create a new file for writing. If the file exists, its contents are overwritten.
"a"Append — open a file for writing. New data is added to the end without overwriting existing content.

After processing, the file should be closed to release system resources and ensure data is saved.

Reading from a file

# Read entire file as a single string
file = open("data.txt", "r")
content = file.read()
print(content)
file.close()

# Read line by line
file = open("data.txt", "r")
for line in file:
    print(line.strip())    # strip() removes trailing newline
file.close()

# Read all lines into a list
file = open("data.txt", "r")
lines = file.readlines()   # each line is a list element
file.close()

Writing to a file

file = open("output.txt", "w")
file.write("First line\n")
file.write("Second line\n")
file.close()

Common mistake

Opening a file in write mode ("w") erases all existing content. If you want to add to an existing file without losing its contents, use append mode ("a") instead.

Appending to a file

file = open("log.txt", "a")
file.write("New entry added\n")
file.close()

Append mode adds new content after the existing data.

Using with for safe file handling

The with statement automatically closes the file when the block ends, even if an error occurs:

with open("data.txt", "r") as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line.strip())
# file is automatically closed here

This is the recommended pattern because it prevents resource leaks.

Worked example

Reading scores from a file and calculating the average

Suppose scores.txt contains one integer per line:

85
92
78
95
88
total = 0
count = 0

with open(“scores.txt”, “r”) as file:
for line in file:
score = int(line.strip())
total += score
count += 1


average = total / count
print(f”Average: {average}”)  # Average: 87.6

Each line is stripped of whitespace, converted to an integer, and accumulated. The file is automatically closed after the with block.

Worked example

Writing results to a CSV file

students = [
    ("Alice", 85),
    ("Bob", 92),
    ("Charlie", 78)
]

with open(“results.csv”, “w”) as file:
file.write(“Name,Score\n”)
for name, score in students:
file.write(f”{name},{score}\n”)

This creates a comma-separated values file that can be opened in a spreadsheet application.

Key takeaways — B2.5.1

  • Files provide persistent storage — data survives after the program ends.
  • Three file modes: read ("r"), write ("w" — overwrites), append ("a" — adds to end).
  • Always close files after use, or use with statements for automatic closing.
  • Write mode erases existing content — use append mode to preserve it.
  • strip() removes trailing newlines when reading line by line.
